extracted.intended_audience: energy lawyers, regulators, compliance officers, grid operators, and policymakers interested in FERC/NERC reliability jurisdiction and registration
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the statutory, regulatory, and procedural standards that determine what facilities and entities fall within FERC/NERC reliability jurisdiction (the "bulk-power system" / "bulk electric system") and the registration/compliance criteria (including treatment of inverter-based resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of "bulk-power system" (FPA §215) / exclusion of local distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress defined the term "bulk-power system" in FPA section 215, but the statutory definition is broad brush and explicitly provides that the term does not include facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory exclusion for local distribution maintains consistency with state regulation of local distribution. However, the broad statutory definition leaves ample room for questions about what is included and what is not; facilities used in local distribution are excluded, but owners/operators of local distribution facilities might nonetheless be jurisdictional as "users" if they otherwise meet the functional criteria. Stakes are high because entities deemed users/owners/operators of the bulk-power system must comply with reliability standards and face substantial monetary penalties (statutory and inflation-adjusted caps discussed in Order No. 672 and later orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC's descriptive test for a "User of the Bulk-Power System" (Order No. 672)
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC offered that '[g]enerally, a person directly connected to the Bulk-Power System selling, purchasing, or transmitting electric energy over the Bulk-Power System is a User of the Bulk-Power System.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC declined to adopt a rigid definition of 'user' in Order No. 672 but clarified that an 'owner or operator of a local distribution facility' that is a 'user' must comply with relevant Reliability Standards; by contrast, a retail customer that only receives retail service and does not directly sell/purchase/transmit over the Bulk-Power System is not a user. FERC warned against definitions that are overly broad (sweeping in too many entities) or overly narrow (excluding those that affect reliability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of generating facilities when their energy is needed for reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC: 'If electric energy from a generating facility is needed to maintain a reliable transmission system, that facility is part of the Bulk-Power System with respect to the energy it generates that is needed to maintain reliability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC reserved judgment on the full scope of generators until standards were proposed in context. The practical effect is that a generating facility can be jurisdictional for the portion of its output that is needed to maintain transmission reliability even if the facility might not otherwise be treated as part of the bulk electric system.

rubrics_metrics.name: NERC 'bulk electric system' core definition and bright-line 100 kV threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: NERC's revised 'core' definition: 'Unless modified by the [inclusion and exclusion] lists shown below, all Transmission Elements operated at 100 kV or higher and Real Power and Reactive Power resources connected at 100 kV or higher. This does not include facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC in Order No. 743 directed elimination of regional discretion, maintenance of a bright-line threshold including all facilities operated at or above 100 kV, and establishment of an exemption process/criteria to exclude facilities not necessary for operating the interconnected transmission network. NERC later preserved the 100 kV core and added specified inclusions/exclusions to address corner cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: NERC Inclusions I2 and I4 (generator and dispersed resource thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion I2: registration of generating resources connected at 100 kV or above with either a gross individual nameplate rating above 20 MVA or a gross plant/facility nameplate rating greater than 75 MVA. Inclusion I4: dispersed power producing resources that aggregate to a total capacity greater than 75 MVA and are connected through a system designed primarily for delivering such capacity to a common point of connection at 100 kV or above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inclusion criteria are technical mechanisms to ensure that significant generators and aggregated dispersed resources (e.g., wind, solar) are captured by the bulk electric system registration. They function as objective thresholds to limit ad hoc, region-varying classifications; NERC's approach also provided for exemptions where justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: NERC Statement of Compliance Registry Criteria (functional categories and thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Registry Criteria identifies categories of transmission grid stakeholders based on function (generator owner, generator operator, transmission owner, transmission operator, balancing authority, etc.) and identifies thresholds for some functional categories (e.g., individual generator units operated above 20 MVA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Registry Criteria includes a 'materiality' provision: '[a]ny entity reasonably deemed material to the reliability of the [Bulk-Power System] will be registered, irrespective of other considerations.' Each Reliability Standard also has an 'Applicability' provision identifying which functional categories must comply. NERC's registration process (voluntary self-identification, Regional Entity notices, appeals) and FERC oversight (appeals to FERC) provide the operational pathway for determining who must comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality provision for registration (individual and aggregate contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: NERC's Registry Criteria materiality clause: any entity reasonably deemed material to reliability will be registered; FERC expanded this to permit registration based on aggregated material impact for inverter-based resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally applied to individual entities, FERC recognized evidence (NERC event reports) that multiple small inverter-based resources could, in aggregate, materially affect Bulk-Power System performance. FERC therefore directed registration of unregistered inverter-based resources connected to the Bulk-Power System that 'in the aggregate have a material impact on Bulk-Power System performance.' This marks a shift from individual-only materiality to acceptance of aggregate-impact registration in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption process and FERC oversight (Order No. 773)
rubrics_metrics.description: NERC's revised BES definition included an exemption process to exclude facilities that meet the core definition but are not necessary for reliable operation; FERC approved the revised definition but directed two tweaks to the exclusion language and approved the exemption process, while reserving the jurisdictional question of 'used in local distribution' to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NERC may entertain petitions about whether facilities satisfy the BES definition, but FERC will receive applications on the jurisdictional question of whether facilities are used in local distribution and will apply the Seven Factor Test (and other factors as appropriate) in making such determinations. FERC retains authority to designate facilities as elements of the BES independent of NERC (though it has not exercised that authority to date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven Factor Test for determining 'used in local distribution'
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC will apply the Seven Factor Test (as used in other contexts) to determine whether facilities are used in local distribution and therefore excluded from section 215 jurisdiction, while considering additional relevant factors in particular situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order No. 773 indicated FERC would make the ultimate determination about whether facilities are used in local distribution, applying the Seven Factor Test with an emphasis that other factors may be considered case-by-case. This provides a flexible but structured legal test for adjudicating borderline classification questions (examples include the Astoria 138 kV facilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC caution about defining 'user' and reliance on NERC registration initially
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC declined to rigidly define 'user of the Bulk-Power System' (concerned that a fixed definition could be too broad or too narrow) and stated it would 'rely on the NERC definition of bulk electric system and NERC's registration process' for an initial period to provide certainty about applicability and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC's approach was pragmatic: defer to NERC's technical registration machinery to identify entities subject to Reliability Standards, while preserving FERC's authority to decide borderline jurisdictional questions. The conceptual distinction was pictured as concentric circles: the bulk-power system (outer, statutory limit of FERC jurisdiction) and NERC's bulk electric system (inner, technical registration boundary generally at 100 kV).

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC monetary penalty exposure and sanction guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Entities subject to Reliability Standards are exposed to potential monetary penalties for violations (Order No. 672 allowed the ERO to propose ranges up to statutory caps; later orders and inflation adjustments set maximums — e.g., referenced maximum daily penalty figures and NERC sanction guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The risk of substantial civil penalties underscores the importance of accurate registration and compliance determinations. The text references statutory caps and inflation-adjusted maximums (e.g., up to approximately $1.58M per violation per day per Order No. 906 (2025) and NERC sanction guidelines figures). This context functions as an enforcement incentive to resolve definitional and registration issues carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration process mechanics and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: NERC's registration process initially encouraged voluntary self-identification; Regional Entities sent letters to inform stakeholders of the intent to register them and applicable functional categories; NERC developed an internal appeals process with appeals to FERC available to those disagreeing with their registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The registry has historically included roughly 1,200–1,400 entities (spiking to over 1,800 after FERC-driven pushes to register inverter-based resources). NERC updates its registry at least monthly. Approximately 35 registration appeals were addressed by NERC since 2007, with roughly 10 petitions for FERC review, concentrated in earlier years. The process creates administrative pathways to resolve classification disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of inverter-based resources (IBRs): operational and registration standards
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC found that mandatory Reliability Standards needed updating to address IBR operational performance (ride-through of minor system disturbances), modeling and planning, and information sharing; and directed NERC to identify and register owners/operators of IBRs connected to the Bulk-Power System that, in the aggregate, have a material impact on reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERC recognized NERC reports showing IBRs tripping or momentarily ceasing in unison, producing material reliability impacts. As remedies, FERC directed NERC to submit a plan, approved that plan, and approved revised Registry Criteria creating Category 2 GO/GOP thresholds for IBR registration. The revised thresholds capture IBRs that contribute to an aggregate nameplate capacity >=20 MVA connected to a common point >=60 kV, intending to subject ~97.5% of Bulk-Power System IBRs to registration and compliance. FERC emphasized this applies only to IBRs connected to the Bulk-Power System (not distribution-level IBRs), although it did not categorically rule out future measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate impact approach for registration (IBRs and similar cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC endorsed registering resources that, while individually small, 'in the aggregate have a material impact on Bulk-Power System performance,' relying on NERC event reports and growth trends to support aggregated impact concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach permits regulators to address distributed, smaller-scale resources whose collective behavior can threaten reliability (e.g., synchronous tripping or momentary cessation). Commenters questioned the factual basis for aggregation; FERC relied on documented events and projections. The aggregate approach is a novel extension of materiality beyond single-entity analysis and is likely to be applied further as the resource mix changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'bulk-power system' and 'bulk electric system' (jurisdictional reach)
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC stated that 'Bulk-Power System reaches farther than those facilities that are included in NERC's definition of the bulk electric system,' conceptually represented as concentric circles where the statutory bulk-power system is the outer circle and NERC's bulk electric system (with general 100 kV threshold) is the inner circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction clarifies that NERC's technical registration boundary is not dispositive of FERC's statutory jurisdiction; FERC may determine jurisdiction beyond NERC's core definition in particular cases. Practically, FERC relied on NERC initially but reserved the ability to interpret/expand jurisdictional scope.
